Remember that integration is the opposite of differentiation. So, if ${F}^{′}(x)=f(x),$ then integrating both sides of this equation gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{F}^{′}(x) & =f(x) \\ \int {F}^{′}(x)\,\text{d}x & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\ F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x.\end{aligned}
$$

We apply the power rule with $n=13$, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}F(x) & =\int f(x)\,\text{d}x \\  & =\int {x}^{13}\,\text{d}x \\  & =\frac{{x}^{13+1}}{13+1}+C \\  & =\frac{{x}^{14}}{14}+C.\end{aligned}
$$

Let's check by differentiating:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{14}}{14}+C) & = \\ \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{{x}^{14}}{14})+\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(C) & = \\ \frac{1}{14}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({x}^{14})+0 & = \\ \frac{1}{14}\cdot 14\,{x}^{13} & = \\ {x}^{13}\,✓\end{aligned}
$$
